extracted.intended_audience: photographers, anthropologists, and researchers interested in composite portraiture and pictorial-statistical methods
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and evaluative principles for producing and interpreting photographic or optical composite portraits (averaged/generic images) from multiple component portraits, including apparatus, registration, exposure, selection of components, and statistical interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of component portraits (size & attitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The photographs must be similar in attitude and size; 'they must be similar in attitude and size, but no exactness is necessary in either of these respects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer components taken in the same aspect and under the same conditions of light and shade. Small differences can be managed (foreshortening, small size differences), but greater heterogeneity complicates alignment and can produce poor composites. Use scaling and slight spatial adjustments (placing larger farther away, inclining for foreshortening) to match sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration / alignment of key reference points (eyes etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Components should be registered so that the eyes (or another selected feature) are as nearly as possible superimposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make two pinholes (register marks) corresponding to cross-threads to hang portraits on the same pair of pins so that pupils coincide. Alternative: use needles on hinged arm to register any desired feature (nose, ear, hand). Accurate registration produces distinct eyes and keeps other features correspondingly aligned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homogeneity of the component group (generic selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composites should be formed from a 'generic' group — individuals who cluster towards a common centre; do not combine heterogeneous elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only combine portraits from the same 'genus' or generic group; combining heterogeneous elements yields monstrous and meaningless results. The group should have a prevalence of mediocre characteristics rather than widely divergent extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of components and statistical averaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Using many components reinforces common traits and causes individual peculiarities to disappear; composites approximate statistical averages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more components that share the common type, the more the composite represents the average (analogy to totals divided by number of cases). Small groups may suffice if they cluster strongly; very large numbers make accessory artifacts vanish. Evidence: 1000 brief exposures ≈ single long exposure of same total duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure strategy for photographic composites (successive exposures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obtain the composite by successively throwing each component's image onto the same sensitised plate for a fraction of the total exposure (sum of brief exposures equals required total exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if one portrait requires 80s, expose eight portraits each 10s to total 80s. In practice better to allow equal time to all components; unequal exposures can bias results. Trials showed equal time to components gives better composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of outline blur as variance
rubrics_metrics.description: The breadth/amount of blur in the composite's outlines measures the tendency of components to deviate from the common type; the band darkest in middle where components agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the darkness and sharpness of areas statistically: outlines/shadows that are common to many components appear sharp and dark; individual peculiarities fade. Use blur as a quantitative visual measure of dispersion from the central type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of optical superimposition instruments (stereoscope, prisms, lanterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Optical methods — stereoscope, double-image prism, converging magic-lanterns, mirrors, divided lenses, sextant arrangements — can be used to superimpose images for optical composites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stereoscope is a makeshift (relies on brain fusion) and can have unequal vividness between eyes; a double-image prism (Iceland spar) or converging magic-lanterns create true optical combinations and are preferable. Adjust prism inclination to vary divergence; multiple prisms can create 4 or 8 images but too many reduces distinctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus configuration and practical ergonomics
rubrics_metrics.description: An apparatus with fixed dark-slide area, a traveling carriage for lens (bellows), and an eye-hole for adjustment allows convenient, accurate management of alignment and exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design apparatus so adjustments are within easy arm's reach; move lens by pinion and rack-work for precision. Use frames with different lenses, mirrors, and clampable arms to pin and incline components; cork-covered floors help pin portraits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale standardisation for comparative materials (coins/medals/historical portraits)
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining small objects (coins, medals) photograph them to uniform scale (e.g., four-tenths of an inch between pupils and lips was used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse photographs when necessary to ensure consistent orientation. Uniform scaling makes composites more reliable for historical likeness reconstruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lens and aperture choices for adjustment vs final photography
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a lens/aperture appropriate to the task: wide aperture for easy adjustment (plenty of light), smaller aperture for final photography (better photographic quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid dry plates under small aperture and specified lighting may require long total exposure (e.g., ~60s in Galton's setup). Wide-aperture lens expedites visual adjustment but smaller aperture improves the photographic result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing size/pose differences (foreshortening and asymmetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits of different sizes or poses can be matched by placing the larger farther, inclining a portrait to foreshorten, or viewing by reflection to reverse profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lenses of different powers or inclined frames to correct size; use mirrors to combine a right profile with a left profile. Slight focus faults from these adjustments are tolerable and produce little ill effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification & comparison of optical vs photographic composites
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate photographic composites by comparing them with optical composites produced live (e.g., magic-lantern superposition); close agreement verifies photographic fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display both side-by-side; also compare composites made from different combinations/permutations of the same components to check robustness. Trials with permutations showed little material difference if exposures are properly managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of target features for registration beyond eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: Although eyes are commonly used for registration, any desired feature (nose, ear, hand, buttons) may be selected as registration reference depending on purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hinged arm with needles or cross-thread register to pin features precisely. Choose the feature that best represents the anatomical correspondence needed for the study (e.g., profile features for profiles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive cautions and intended use (composites as generalisations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composites are not portraits of individuals but ideal, averaged representatives of a class; they are 'pictorial statistics' and analogues of blended memories or generic images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composites to study typical traits of a group (e.g., criminal types, family traits, historical likenesses). Remember composites may be 'better looking' than components because individual irregularities average out; treat results as generalisations, not identifications.
